result: T2*-weighted MRI detected cerebral microbleeds as early as day 4 post-infection in the turbinates and olfactory bulb (OB), with bleeding increasing through day 11. Microbleeds were observed in specific OB layers (ONL, GL, GCL) and spread from frontal brain to midbrain, with ~100-fold greater bleeding density in the OB compared to other brain regions. These microbleeds co-localized with sites of VSV replication.
evaluation: Claims C4, C26-C33, C36-C41 are well-supported by MRI data (Figures 1-2) showing temporal progression and spatial distribution of microbleeds, with quantitative measurements and histological verification. The co-localization with viral replication sites is demonstrated through immunohistochemistry.

result: VSV-induced microbleeds occurred independently of peripheral immune cell infiltration. Blocking immune cell entry with anti-LFA-1/VLA-4 antibodies reduced CD45+ cells by >95% but increased bleeding volume in turbinates (2.1±0.8 to 5.0±1.0 mm³) and doubled brain bleeding spots, while also elevating viral RNA 2-3-fold. Vascular endothelial activation (VCAM-1/ICAM-1 upregulation) was observed at bleeding sites.
evaluation: Claims C5, C43-C56 are strongly supported by antibody blockade experiments (Figure 3) with quantitative MRI, flow cytometry showing >95% immune cell depletion, and RT-qPCR data. The paradoxical increase in bleeding when immune cells are blocked demonstrates that peripheral immune cells are not required for, and actually protect against, VSV-induced vascular damage.

result: VSV infected vascular endothelial cells in cerebral blood vessels, with some infected vessels showing evidence of bleeding. VSV G-protein binds LDL-R, which is expressed on brain capillary endothelium, and VSV-GFP can infect and lyse endothelial cells in culture.
evaluation: Claims C60-C62, C114-C116 are supported by immunohistochemical data (Figure 4) showing VSV in CD31+ endothelial cells with associated bleeding, and by citations to prior literature establishing the LDL-R entry mechanism. However, C62 is appropriately cautious ('may contribute') as direct causation is not definitively proven.

result: Adoptive transfer of 5×10⁵ virus-specific CD8+ OT-I T cells at early (day 0-2) or late (day 6) stages reduced cerebral microbleeds and viral RNA. For late-stage transfer, bleeding volume in turbinates decreased from 12.2±1.3 to 1.6±1.1 mm³, OB hypointensity spots decreased from 665±127 to 114±23, and brain spots decreased from 329±72 to 83±19 on day 11. Early transfer reduced viral RNA from 0.95±0.37 to 0.29±0.07.
evaluation: Claims C63-C70, C118, C133 are well-supported by quantitative MRI data (Figure 5) and RT-qPCR measurements showing therapeutic benefit of T cell transfer at both early and late stages. Statistical significance is reported (p<0.0001) with appropriate sample sizes (n=5-7).

result: Immunohistochemistry confirmed that T cell transfer increased CD8+ T cells and reduced VSV and microbleeds in the GL and OB center. However, some microbleeds persisted in regions with high T cell density, and administering excessive T cells (3×10⁶ vs. 5×10⁵) was pathogenic, increasing bleeding. This demonstrates the need for a precise balance between viral control and tissue preservation.
evaluation: Claims C71-C77, C134-C135 are supported by immunohistochemical quantification (Figure 6) and dose-response data (Figure 6—supplement 1) showing that while therapeutic doses of T cells reduce pathology, excessive doses cause harm. This establishes an important dose-dependent relationship.

result: A method was developed to label CD8+ T cells with MPIO particles modified with cationic amine groups and anti-CD3 for enhanced uptake. The labeling yield was ~8.3%, with 91% of MPIOs localized intracellularly. MPIO-labeled T cells showed single-cell MRI detection sensitivity and retained normal migration, IL-2/IFN-γ release, and therapeutic function in vivo.
evaluation: Claims C7, C78-C85, C120-C121 are well-supported by FACS data (Figure 7B), electron microscopy (Figure 7E), MRI sensitivity measurements (Figure 7F), and functional assays (Figure 7G, supplements). The preservation of therapeutic function is demonstrated by comparing bleeding reduction in mice receiving labeled vs. unlabeled T cells.

result: MPIO-labeled virus-specific CD8+ T cells were detected in the brain by MRI as early as 22-24 hours post-infection. At 24 hr, hypointensities appeared in the GL (where T cells and bleeding co-localized, with 85% of T cells in bleeding regions) and MCL/GCL (where hypointensities were due only to T cells without bleeding). No T cell migration between these regions was detected by time-lapse MRI, suggesting local extravasation.
evaluation: Claims C8, C86-C96, C123 are supported by time-lapse MRI (Figure 8I, Videos 1-2) and immunohistochemistry (Figure 8D-H) distinguishing T cell signals from bleeding. The quantification showing 85% of T cells in bleeding regions vs. 15% in non-bleeding regions (Figure 8H) is well-documented. However, the inability to detect migration (C94, C96) is a negative result with inherent limitations.

result: At day 1 post-infection, vascular endothelial activation (VCAM-1/ICAM-1) and microglial activation (CD68) were detected at sites where CD8 T cells and microbleeds co-localized. The combination of MPIO-labeled T cells and bleeding increased MRI sensitivity for detecting neuroinflammation sites through additive contrast effects.
evaluation: Claims C97-C100 are supported by immunohistochemical data (Figure 8J) showing co-localization of multiple inflammatory markers, and by quantitative MRI data (Figure 8—supplement 2C,D) demonstrating increased detection sensitivity when both T cells and bleeding are present. This validates the dual-contrast approach for neuroinflammation imaging.

result: The study leverages established principles of T2*-weighted MRI sensitivity to microbleeds. VSV viral titers in the OB reach ~10⁴ PFU on day 1 and peak at ~10⁵ PFU on day 6. The OB comprises ~2% of brain volume. MRI can detect ~1 pg iron per voxel, equivalent to ~5-10 fully deoxygenated RBCs (0.2 pg iron each), enabling detection within 2 days compared to 1-2 weeks for CT.
evaluation: Claims C34-C35, C42, C101-C107 are supported by citations to established literature and prior studies. The viral titer data (C34-C35) is confirmed by the current study's RT-qPCR (Figure 1F). The MRI sensitivity calculations are based on well-established physics principles and prior literature, providing context for the method's capabilities.

result: Following intranasal inoculation, VSV replicates in the lung, causes transient viremia, and is found transiently in liver and spleen, but is cleared from the periphery within 2-3 days. The authors infer that direct CNS infection, rather than peripheral pathology, causes brain microbleeds in this model based on the temporal pattern.
evaluation: Claims C111-C112 are supported by citations to prior literature. Claim C113 is an inference appropriately qualified by the authors ('we think'). The temporal correlation between CNS viral replication (peaking day 6) and microbleeds, combined with peripheral clearance by day 2-3, supports this interpretation, though the authors acknowledge no direct experiments ruled out peripheral contributions.

result: The peripheral immune response is important for maintaining vascular integrity and pathogen clearance, as demonstrated by increased bleeding and viral RNA when immune cell entry was blocked. However, transferred CD8+ T cells were not completely effective at blocking early viral entry from olfactory sensory neurons into the OB, and vascular damage worsens when peripheral immune infiltration is blocked.
evaluation: Claims C117, C119, C132 are supported by the antibody blockade experiments (Figure 3) and T cell transfer studies (Figure 5). C119 is an appropriate inference from the observation that some bleeding occurred even with early T cell transfer. The claims accurately reflect the dual role of immune responses in both protection and potential pathology.

result: VSV showed tropism for neurons in the GL and GCL, which contain proliferating immature neurons in rodents. These neurons are generated in the subventricular zone and traffic through the rostral migratory stream to the OB. Many viruses have tropism for immature neurons, which may partially explain VSV's tropism. CD8+ T cells control neuronal virus through engagements with cross-presenting microglia.
evaluation: Claims C122-C128 are supported by immunohistochemical data showing VSV distribution and citations to prior literature on OB neurogenesis and viral tropism. C128 is appropriately speculative ('may in part explain'). C124 is supported by citation to prior work. The claims provide biological context for the observed spatial patterns of infection.

result: MRI can be used to evaluate the extent of pathology after CNS viral infection and the efficacy of therapeutic interventions like adoptive antiviral T cell transfer.
evaluation: Claims C137-C138 are supported by the comprehensive MRI data throughout the study demonstrating longitudinal monitoring of pathology (Figures 1-2) and therapeutic response (Figure 5). This represents a valid conclusion about the utility of the imaging approach developed in this work.

result: The introduction and discussion provide context from prior literature on CNS infections, viral entry mechanisms, immune responses, MRI detection methods, and clinical relevance. This includes established knowledge about CNS infection morbidity, viral entry routes, immune cell roles, T cell behavior, microbleed detection by MRI, and clinical implications for stroke, TBI, and COVID-19.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C10-C25, C108-C110, C129-C130, C136 are appropriately supported by citations to prior literature and represent established knowledge in the field. These claims provide necessary background and context for the current study but do not represent novel findings from this work.

result: The study used a murine model where VSV was introduced intranasally and entered the brain via olfactory sensory neurons through retrograde trans-neuronal transport, spreading via both anterograde and retrograde transport. Most VSV-infected neurons are cleared noncytolytically despite VSV being highly cytopathic.
evaluation: Claims C3, C57-C59 describe the experimental model and are supported by the methods section and citations to prior literature (Beier et al., 2013; Cornish et al., 2001; Moseman et al., 2020). This establishes the biological basis for the infection model used throughout the study.
